design_detail: Descriptive monitoring report of the Dutch Drug Information and Monitoring System (DIMS): laboratory results for 33,006 tablets sold as ecstasy that people handed in anonymously at 25 test offices across the Netherlands from January 1993 to December 2008 and that were analysed in the laboratory (thin-layer chromatography, gas chromatography with nitrogen–phosphorus detection for known compounds, GC–MS for unknown ones) (PDF pp. 2–4). Tablets identified at the test office from their recorded appearance and a Marquis reagent test against a weekly updated recognition list ('quick-testing'), without laboratory analysis, are not part of these results (PDF pp. 3–4). Outcomes by year: share of tablets containing only ecstasy-like substances (MDMA, MDA, MDEA, MBDB), share containing only MDMA ('purity'), MDMA content in five categories with yearly medians, amphetamine and other psychoactive substances (Figures 2–5, Table 1). To test whether DIMS reflects the consumer market, results for 2004–2006 were compared with 4,029 tablets confiscated from people going out and sent by the police to DIMS (Pearson χ², Mann–Whitney U) (PDF pp. 3–4, 7). The online-first PDF was read (see verification). Filed as cross-sectional and appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist, as the round brief directs for drug-checking data.
can_establish: What the tablets sold as ecstasy that people brought to Dutch drug-checking offices, and that were analysed in the laboratory, contained in each year from 1993 to 2008: how often only MDMA or other substances, and how much MDMA; and that tablets seized from people going out in 2004–2006 contained broadly the same substances.
cannot_establish: How reliably a tablet's logo and appearance identify its content (the 99% reliability of the recognition list is asserted from internal investigations without data, PDF p. 3); how much content varies among tablets with the same logo (not reported); the composition of the whole Dutch market (self-selected samples; the authors call DIMS a qualitative monitor, PDF p. 8); or anything about effects or harms.

sample.recruitment: Tablets handed in anonymously by individual (potential) consumers at one of 25 DIMS test offices, most of them part of addiction-care and prevention centres across the Netherlands (PDF p. 2, Methods › The DIMS testing procedure). Comparison sample: samples confiscated in 2004–2006 from people going out to clubs and parties, handed to the police and sent to DIMS (PDF p. 3, Methods › Seized tablets).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Only tablets sold as ecstasy that were analysed in the laboratory: of over 79,000 samples collected in 1993–2008, 33,006 tablets (PDF p. 4). Tablets recognized at the test office without laboratory analysis (on average 30% of tablets, PDF p. 3) and seized tablets are excluded. Yearly totals are printed above Figure 2 (371 in 1993; 1,258 to 2,578 a year from 1994).
sample.demographics: Not collected in this analysis; consumers are anonymous. The introduction gives figures for Dutch adults (lifetime ecstasy use 4.3% in 2005), not for people who use the test offices (PDF p. 1).
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected submissions. The authors attribute the over-representation of low- and high-MDMA tablets and of other active substances among DIMS tablets, compared with seized tablets, to people preferring to submit tablets whose effects differed from what they expected (PDF p. 8). Recognized tablets, which are by definition known types, are excluded, which may over-represent new or unusual tablets. The seized comparison sample is itself selected (people found with drugs while going out).

exposure.measurement: Laboratory analysis at the Delta Psychiatric Hospital laboratory: thin-layer chromatography (Toxilab) to identify main components, capillary gas chromatography with nitrogen–phosphorus detection to identify and quantify known compounds (MDMA, MDEA, MDA, cocaine, heroin, amphetamine, caffeine, methamphetamine), GC–MS for unknown compounds; at least two qualitative and one quantitative analysis per tablet (PDF p. 3, Methods › Laboratory analyses).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable (tablets). MDMA content per tablet grouped as 1–35, 36–70, 71–105, 106–140 and above 140 mg (PDF p. 4).
exposure.polysubstance: Other psychoactive substances counted by year (Table 1, PDF p. 5); medicinal substances such as paracetamol and production intermediates such as piperonal were found sporadically and are not shown (PDF p. 6).

comparison.controls: Seized tablets of 2004–2006 (4,029 tablets for purity and other substances; the 737 MDMA-containing seized tablets analysed in the laboratory for MDMA content) against DIMS tablets of the same years; otherwise comparisons are between years.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not reported: which seized tablets entered the purity comparison (all 4,029, whose contents came largely from recognition against the DIMS database, or only those analysed); the denominators of the seized-tablet percentages in Table 1; the contents of recognized tablets; variation of content within a logo.

outcomes.instruments: Shares of tablets by contents (only ecstasy-like substances; ecstasy-like plus other active substances; only other active substances; no active substance; Figure 2); purity (Figure 3); MDMA content categories and yearly medians (Figure 4); tablets containing amphetamine (Figure 5); counts of other psychoactive substances with mean and range of amounts (Table 1); seized against DIMS tablets (Figure 6 and text) (PDF pp. 4–7).
outcomes.validity_norms: Laboratory methods are described, but no validation data (detection limits, quantification error) are given. The recognition list's 99% reliability is asserted from internal investigations without methods or numbers (PDF p. 3).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Purity' = the share of tablets containing only MDMA as the pharmacologically active substance (PDF p. 4); 'ecstasy-like substances' = MDMA and the analogues MDA, MDEA and MBDB (PDF p. 4).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: three tests (two χ² and one Mann–Whitney U) comparing seized with DIMS tablets; everything else is descriptive.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported (of little concern for laboratory identification; recognition at the test offices rests on staff matching tablets to the list).

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive yearly percentages and medians, without intervals. Seized against DIMS tablets, 2004–2006: only MDMA in 86% against 79% (χ² 89.7, P < 0.01); seized MDMA-containing tablets more often in the 36–105 mg categories (χ² 28.0, P < 0.01); median MDMA 70 mg against 72 mg (Mann–Whitney Z = −0.67, P = 0.503) (PDF p. 7). Editors' calculation from the n printed above Figures 2 and 4: tablets containing any MDMA were 54% (1993), 58% (1994), 57% (1997) and 84% (1998) of laboratory-analysed tablets sold as ecstasy, 94–96% in 2000–2004 and 81% in 2008.
analysis.selective_reporting: Results are limited to laboratory-analysed tablets: recognized tablets, a large share of submissions, are not described, and the recognition list's reliability is reported as one unsupported figure. Medicinal substances and production intermediates are 'data not shown' (PDF p. 6).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 33,006 laboratory-analysed tablets sold as ecstasy in the Netherlands in 1993–2008, the share containing only MDMA ranged from 44% (1997) to about 86% (2000–2004), with MDEA common in 1993–1996 and mCPP rising from 2004; the median MDMA content per tablet ranged from 60 mg (1998) to 84 mg (1994), single tablets from traces to 225 mg, and tablets of 106 mg or more rose to 30% in 2008. Tablets seized from people going out in 2004–2006 contained the same substances, somewhat more often only MDMA, with a similar median MDMA content.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and the closing summary say that DIMS appears to be a market monitor giving an accurate reflection of what is actually available on the hidden Dutch ecstasy market (PDF pp. 1, 9). The discussion itself says DIMS results are not an exact representation of the market and calls DIMS a fairly accurate picture and a fairly valid monitor (PDF p. 8). The validation rests on seized tablets whose contents were obtained largely by matching them to the DIMS database itself (at least 85% recognized immediately, PDF p. 7), so it shows mainly that DIMS already knew the tablets in circulation, not that its content figures are accurate for the market; the purity difference (79% against 86%) is called small although it is statistically significant (PDF p. 7). The 99% reliability of identifying tablets by appearance and a colour test, on which part of the DIMS system rests, is supported only by unpublished internal investigations (PDF p. 3).

timeline.event: Spruit (2001): results of the first five years of DIMS monitoring (1993–1997), which this paper extends (ref. 8, PDF p. 2); not read here.
Parrott (2004): review of the proportion of ecstasy tablets containing MDMA; the authors say the DIMS results are in line with it (ref. 44, PDF p. 8).
This paper (online first; print in 2009, vol. 104).
Brunt and Niesink (2011), from the same programme, extend the series to 2010 and repeat the 99% reliability figure for the recognition list, again without data.
Brunt et al. (2017, TEDI) cite this paper and Brunt and Niesink (2011) for the reliability of DIMS tablet recognition (card sc_brunt_2017).

replication.where_it_stands: A descriptive monitoring series, so replication is not the question. The reliability of identifying tablets by logo, measurements and colour test, which later DIMS publications repeat or cite, has no published data in this paper.

funding.funder: The DIMS project is financed by the Dutch Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (PDF p. 9, Acknowledgements).
funding.affiliations_note: All six authors work in the DIMS programme at the Trimbos Institute (PDF p. 1), the system the paper describes and validates. A flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Publication of the recognition list's validation data: for every tablet first identified by appearance and colour test and then also analysed in the laboratory, whether the main substance and the MDMA amount (within a stated margin) matched the batch record, with the spread of MDMA content within each logo, by year.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Tablets submitted to a national drug-checking network: a frame for what people choose to have tested, not for the market the abstract describes.
Self-selected submissions; recognized tablets excluded; the seized comparison sample is itself selected.
About 2,000 laboratory-analysed tablets a year from 1994 (371 in 1993).

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Procedure, test offices and laboratory are described; nothing is reported about who submits tablets.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: How many tablets sold as ecstasy were recognized instead of analysed, by year, is not given; the seized-tablet percentages imply more tablets than the 4,029 reported.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Thin-layer chromatography, GC with nitrogen–phosphorus detection and GC–MS, with at least two qualitative and one quantitative analysis per tablet.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: One laboratory throughout; whether methods or detection limits changed over 16 years is not stated.

Yearly percentages without intervals suit monitoring, but the text's 78% average does not match Figures 2–3, two Table 1 columns do not add up, and the validation compares partly database-derived values.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A large, single-laboratory series with consistent methods, appropriate for describing what laboratory-analysed DIMS tablets contained year by year; as estimates for the whole Dutch market the risk of bias is higher, because submissions are self-selected, recognized tablets are excluded and the validation against seized tablets is partly circular. Citable for: in the Netherlands in 1993–2008, tablets sold as ecstasy and analysed by DIMS often contained something other than, or besides, MDMA (only MDMA in 44% in 1997 and about 86% in 2000–2004); MDMA content varied from traces to 225 mg per tablet, with yearly medians of 60–84 mg; DIMS identified about 30% of tablets by appearance and colour test against a list of recently analysed tablets. Not citable for: how reliable that identification is, how much tablets with the same logo vary, or the exact composition of the Dutch market.

key_findings.finding: From January 1993 to December 2008 DIMS collected over 79,000 samples; the paper reports the 33,006 tablets sold as ecstasy that were analysed in the laboratory, about 2,000 a year (371 in 1993; between 1,258 and 2,578 a year from 1994), excluding tablets identified without laboratory analysis and seized tablets.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Figure 2 (n per year above the bars)

key_findings.finding: Identification by appearance ('quick-testing'): test-office staff measure each tablet's weight, diameter and thickness and describe its logo, shape, colour and profile; if these (diameter within ±0.10 mm, thickness within ±0.30 mm) and a Marquis reagent test match a known tablet on the weekly updated recognition list, the tablet is 'recognized', its average MDMA content is taken as known, and it need not be analysed. Laboratory results of recognized tablets that consumers still want analysed are used to validate the list; internal investigations are said to show 99% reliability. On average 30% of tablets are determined this way.
key_findings.locator: Methods › The DIMS testing procedure, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 2, right column) and 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 3, left column)
key_findings.note: No methods, period, numbers or definition of reliability are given for the 99% figure (for example whether it concerns the main substance or the MDMA amount), and recognized tablets are excluded from the results, so the paper gives no data on how much content varies among tablets with the same logo.

key_findings.finding: The introduction states, citing other studies, that MDMA analogues and other drugs appear in ecstasy tablets in varying concentrations that are not visible on the outside of the tablets, and that deaths have been reported after tablets sold as ecstasy contained MBDB, PMA or 4-MTA.
On average 78% of tablets contained only ecstasy-like substances (MDMA, MDA, MDEA or MBDB) as the active compound; the lowest share was 60% in 1997, the highest about 92% in 2000 and 2004.
key_findings.locator: Results › Contents and purity of TSX, 1st paragraph; Figure 2
key_findings.note: The yearly shares implied by the n above Figures 2 and 3 average about 82.5%, not 78% (editors' calculation; see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Tablets containing only MDMA as the active substance ('purity'): lowest 44% in 1997, highest in 2000–2004 (86% on average). MDEA alone was in at least 15% of tablets each year in 1993–1996, 8% in 1997 and never above 1% afterwards; MDA alone averaged 2% and virtually disappeared after 2005; MBDB was found only in 1993–1997 (about 1%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Contents and purity of TSX, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 4); Figure 3 (PDF p. 6)
key_findings.note: Read from Figure 3 on a 300-dpi crop (approximate): only MDMA in about 49–50% of tablets in 1993–1994 and about 70% in 2008.

key_findings.finding: Editors' calculation from the n printed above Figures 2 and 4: the share of laboratory-analysed tablets sold as ecstasy that contained any MDMA was 54% in 1993, 58% in 1994, 57% in 1997, 84% in 1998, between 94% and 96% in 2000–2004, and 81% in 2008.
key_findings.locator: Figure 2 (n per year, PDF p. 4); Figure 4 (n of tablets containing MDMA, PDF p. 6)
key_findings.note: Figure 4's n are the tablets that contained MDMA (PDF p. 4, MDMA dosage of TSX); their 2004–2006 total (6,033) equals the n of DIMS tablets in Figure 6, which supports this reading.

key_findings.finding: MDMA content of tablets containing MDMA: the share with 106 mg or more increased gradually from 1998 and was highest in 2008 (30%); the share above 140 mg peaked in 2004 (10%); the median was 73 mg over the whole period, ranging from 60 mg (1998) to 84 mg (1994); single tablets ranged from traces (under 1 mg) to 225 mg.
key_findings.locator: Results › MDMA dosage of TSX, single paragraph (PDF p. 4); Figure 4, medians per year (PDF p. 6)

key_findings.finding: Tablets containing amphetamine (with or without other substances) were considerably fewer from 2000 to 2008 than before 2000; amphetamine content in such tablets ranged from 1 to 65 mg. In the editors' calculation from the n above Figure 5, they were 17.6% of analysed tablets in 1997 and between 1% and 5% a year in 2000–2008.
key_findings.locator: Results › Amphetamine found in TSX, single paragraph (PDF p. 6); Figure 5 (PDF p. 7)

key_findings.finding: Other psychoactive substances (Table 1): caffeine in every year (33 to 520 tablets a year); ephedrine often in 1994–1997; a peak in 1997 (2C-B 100 tablets, atropine 40, methamphetamine 52, caffeine 520); PMA in 2001 (30) and 2002 (8); a second peak in 2006–2008 driven by mCPP (12 tablets in 2004, 72 in 2005, 224 in 2006, 222 in 2007, 310 in 2008) and caffeine.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (PDF p. 5); Results › Other psychoactive substances found in TSX, single paragraph (PDF p. 6)
key_findings.note: Table 1's 'Total (%)' is the number of cases found divided by the tablets analysed that year (for example 769 of 2,344 in 1997); a tablet with two such substances would count twice, so it is not the share of tablets containing other substances.

key_findings.finding: Seized against DIMS tablets, 2004–2006: police sent 15,837 seized samples, including 4,029 tablets, whose contents were obtained by comparison with the DIMS database and/or laboratory analysis; at least 85% were recognized immediately from the database. Only MDMA: 86% of seized against 79% of DIMS tablets (χ² 89.7, P < 0.01). Among MDMA-containing tablets analysed in the laboratory (737 seized, 6,033 DIMS), seized tablets fell more often in the 36–105 mg categories (χ² 28.0, P < 0.01), with similar medians (70 against 72 mg; Mann–Whitney Z = −0.67, P = 0.503). The same other substances were found in both, less often among seized tablets.
key_findings.locator: Results › Seized samples versus TSX, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Figure 6
key_findings.note: Which seized tablets entered the purity comparison is not stated. In the editors' calculation a χ² near 89.7 fits all 4,029 seized tablets (about 61–107 allowing for rounding) but not the 737 analysed ones (about 15–26), so most seized tablets in that comparison were probably given the database's own values.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that DIMS results are not, by definition, an exact representation of the Dutch ecstasy market and that DIMS is a qualitative monitor of contents rather than of quantities; they suggest that the over-representation of low- and high-MDMA tablets and of other active substances among DIMS tablets may be explained by people preferring to submit tablets whose effects differed from what they expected, and conclude that DIMS is a fairly valid monitor of the consumer market. [Hedge restored: 'may be explained by'; the same wording in sample.selection_effects should change too.]

reporting_issues.issue: The text says that on average 78% of tablets contained only ecstasy-like substances (PDF p. 4). In the editors' calculation, the yearly shares implied by the n printed above Figures 2 and 3 average about 82.5%, both as a mean of yearly shares and pooled over all tablets, and the bars of Figure 2 agree.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite yearly values rather than the 78% average.

reporting_issues.issue: Two columns of Table 1 do not add up to their printed totals (205 for 1994, 126 for 2000). In the editors' calculation the 1994 cells sum to 208 (the printed 16.5% fits 208) and the 2000 cells to 129 (the printed 5.1% fits 126).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; a cell or a total is misprinted in each of these years.

reporting_issues.issue: For 2004–2006 Table 1 gives seized-tablet counts with percentages (76 with 3.6%, 28 with 2.4%, 115 with 8.0%), and the text reports 4,029 seized tablets (PDF p. 7). In the editors' calculation the percentages imply about 2,100, 1,170 and 1,440 tablets, about 4,700 in all; the denominators are not given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The seized-tablet percentages cannot be reconciled with the stated sample; cite counts rather than percentages.

reporting_issues.issue: Which seized tablets entered the purity comparison (86% against 79%) is not stated: the contents of the 4,029 seized tablets were obtained by matching to the DIMS database and/or laboratory analysis, with at least 85% recognized from the database, whereas the MDMA-content comparison used only the 737 analysed in the laboratory (Figure 6). In the editors' calculation the χ² of 89.7 fits about 4,000 seized tablets, not 737.
reporting_issues.consequence: The validation against seized tablets is partly circular: it supports the claim that DIMS knows the tablets in circulation more than the claim that its content figures are accurate for the market.

reporting_issues.issue: The 99% reliability of the recognition list and the 30% of tablets determined by recognition are given without methods, period, numbers or a definition of reliability.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper gives no basis for claims about how reliably a tablet's logo and appearance identify its content.

reporting_issues.issue: The period 1993–2008 is called 16 years in the abstract and discussion but 15 years in three places in the results.
The 'predominant mode of action' column of Table 1 is taken from a drug-information website (erowid.org, Table 1 footnote), not from cited pharmacological studies.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; do not cite that column for pharmacology.

verification.source_read: PDF (online-first version, Addiction, doi 10.1111/j.1360-0443.2009.02707.x, without volume or final pagination; pages numbered 1–10; submitted 22 December 2008, accepted 4 June 2009): all pages (text PDF pp. 1–9, references pp. 9–10); every number checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi; Table 1 (a landscape page) checked on 220-dpi crops; Figures 2–6 read on the rendered pages, with Figure 3 also on a 300-dpi crop (the printed n and medians and the text values are used; bar heights only where marked approximate); no supplement. The PDF prints thousands with a space (33 006, 79 000, 15 837), written here with commas. Not the version of record (vol. 104, issue 12, pp. 2057–2066): anchors give PDF pages, which differ from the printed pages.

disagreements.reviewer: The authors state that DIMS results are not, by definition, an exact representation of the Dutch ecstasy market and that DIMS is a qualitative monitor of contents rather than of quantities; they suggest that the over-representation of low- and high-MDMA tablets and of other active substances among DIMS tablets may be explained by people preferring to submit tablets whose effects differed from what they expected, and conclude that DIMS is a fairly valid monitor of the consumer market. [Hedge restored: 'may be explained by'; the same wording in sample.selection_effects should change too.]
disagreements.resolution: Second reader's correction adopted by the AI co-editor (AI reader 771 (round-2 check))

disagreements.reviewer: The Discussion adds that no substance was found among the seized tablets that DIMS did not already know (p. 8), which bears on the circularity point. It also says, citing reference 51, that many people who test their tablets adjust their use to the result (p. 9). This is a cited statement, not data from this study.
disagreements.resolution: Recorded for the card's next revision; not yet in the card.
